The nested estimate measures how well a whole tuning procedure (resample,
tune, select, fit) performs on new data. This page says what it describes,
what to report, and how far to trust it.

This page runs no code. The worked example is in `vignette("nested-cv")`.

## Why the tuned score is optimistic

When we tune with cross-validation, we score several candidates (the
settings tried) and keep the best. Scores are noisy, and the best of
several noisy numbers tends to look better than it is. So the winner's
score overstates how the model will do on new data.

Nested resampling moves the tuning inside each outer fold. Each fold
tunes, selects and fits on its own analysis rows, then scores the chosen
setting once on assessment rows that the tuning never saw.

## What the estimate describes

The mean from `collect_metrics()` is the error of the procedure when it
trains on each fold's analysis rows and is scored on fresh data. Bayle et
al. (2026) call this the k-fold test error of the procedure.

The estimate describes the procedure, not one fitted model, and we report
it for the deployed model because `nested_final_fit()` runs that procedure
on all the data. No rows remain that the final fit did not see, so there
is no second number to compute.

The estimate is not a score of the parameter values the final fit chose.
It is also the error on this data set, not the average over every training
set the same source can produce. Luo and Barber (2026) prove that any
assumption-free test of that average needs far more data than the
training set holds.

## Where a test set fits

Every outer score already comes from rows the tuning never saw, so nested
resampling can stand in for a held-out test set. With enough data, we can
still keep one. We split with `initial_split()` and run the nested loop
and `nested_final_fit()` on `training()`. Then we score the final model's
predictions on `testing()` once, as `last_fit()` does after ordinary
tuning.

The two numbers answer different questions. The test score is one number
for one fitted model. The nested estimate describes the procedure that
made it.

## Choosing the number of folds

No fold count is best for every problem. Arlot and Celisse (2010) report
that 5 to 10 folds is the usual advice when the goal is an estimate. More
outer folds give each model more training rows, and each outer fold adds a
whole tuning run. For a grid, the tuning fits number the product of the
two fold counts and the grid size.

## A slight pessimism

Each outer model trains on fewer rows than the deployed model, so the
estimate tends to look a little worse than the procedure deserves. Varma
and Simon (2006) ran nested cross-validation on null data with 40 samples.
The true error was 50.0%, and the nested estimate was 54.2%.

Wilimitis and
Walsh (2023) found it among the most pessimistic methods on 41,121
hospital visits. This gap is no reason to adjust the reported number.

## The standard error

`std_err` is the standard deviation of the outer scores divided by the
square root of their number. It measures the precision of the mean, not
the spread of the folds. It is not a confidence interval. Bengio and
Grandvalet (2004) prove that no estimator of a k-fold estimate's variance
is unbiased in every case.

## Comparing workflows

A gap between two nested estimates is a reason to look closer, never a
result. Bayle et al. (2026) show that two procedures can each be stable
while their difference is not, so an interval for the difference can fail.
Picking the best of a set from `nested_workflow_map()` is itself a
selection that no outer loop scored.

## When the folds disagree

When the folds choose different values for a parameter, the data does not
pin that value down. The estimate still holds, because it averages over
that variation. As two candidates' predictions converge, which one wins a
fold comes close to a coin flip (Bayle et al., 2026).

## When nesting pays

Nesting matters most when the search had room to overfit. Tibshirani and
Tibshirani (2009) tuned on pure noise with a true error of 0.5. With 400
rows and 100 features, the tuned score was under 3 points too good.
With 40 rows and 1000 features, one learner read 0.384, 11.6 points too
good.

Nesting adds little for tall data and a small grid. Wilimitis and Walsh
(2023) found no gain on 41,121 visits, at a cost that grew with the square
of the fold count.

Small data is not safe either. Vabalas et al. (2019)
saw cross-validation without nesting report better than chance on pure
noise at 1000 rows.

Feature selection belongs in the recipe, so the loop repeats it in every
fold. Vabalas et al. (2019) found that a selection step outside the loop
does more harm than tuning outside it.

for model selection. *Statistics Surveys*, 4, 40–79.

Bayle, A., Janson, L., & Mackey, L. (2026). The relative instability of

minimum error rate in cross-validation. *The Annals of Applied

learning algorithm validation with a limited sample size. *PLoS ONE*,

cross-validation for model selection. *BMC Bioinformatics*, 7, 91.

examples of cross-validation for model development and evaluation in
